# SDK Client Convention

Ensure consistency for every third-party SDK wrapper ("client"). Vocabulary comes from [vocabulary-convention.md](../../core/vocabulary-convention.md).

A client's job is to own one SDK connection and expose the operations the application actually uses. It knows nothing about HTTP, the web framework, or where its configuration came from.

## Scope

Applies to files named `*.client.ts` and anything under a `clients/` directory.

Does **not** apply to:

- Service classes, which hold business logic — see [repository-convention.md § Layering](./repository-convention.md#layering).
- Repositories — see [repository-convention.md](./repository-convention.md).
- The app's composition root, which reads env and constructs clients, and nothing more.

## Location & File Naming

One client per file, kebab-case, singular: `{client_name}.client.ts`.

Name the file after the **SDK or service**, not the role it plays in the app. The role is the consumer's concern and it changes; the SDK does not.

```
// CORRECT
s3.client.ts
ses.client.ts
redlock.client.ts

// WRONG — named after the role
storage.client.ts
mailer.client.ts
lock.client.ts
```

## Class & Config Naming

Each file exports exactly **one** primary class `{ClientName}Client`, matching the file name, plus its config type `{ClientName}Config`. Config is a `type`, not an `interface`.

```ts
// CORRECT — s3.client.ts
export type S3Config = { ... };
export class S3Client { ... }

// WRONG — class name does not match the file name
// s3.client.ts
export class StorageClient { ... }

// WRONG — role baked into the class name
export class SesMailClient { ... }

// WRONG — config declared as an interface
export interface SesConfig { ... }
```

### Name collisions with the SDK

When the SDK exports the same name, **alias the vendor import**. Never rename our class to dodge the collision — the class name is dictated by the file name.

```ts
// CORRECT — s3.client.ts
import { PutObjectCommand, S3Client as AwsS3Client } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';

export class S3Client {
  private _client: AwsS3Client | null;
}

// WRONG — our class renamed to make room for the vendor's
import { S3Client } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';

export class StorageClient { ... }
```

## Constructor

Signature is always `(config, logger)` — config first, logger second. The config parameter is named after its type in camelCase.

Destructure the config on the first line of the body, then assign fields one per line.

```ts
// CORRECT
export class SesClient {
  private _client: SESv2Client;
  private _fromAddress: string;
  private _logger: Logger;

  constructor(sesConfig: SesConfig, logger: Logger) {
    const { sesClientConfig, fromName, fromEmail } = sesConfig;

    this._client = new SESv2Client(sesClientConfig);
    this._fromAddress = SesClient.formatFromAddress(fromName, fromEmail);
    this._logger = logger;
  }
}

// WRONG — logger folded into the config
constructor(sesConfig: SesConfig & { logger: Logger }) { ... }

// WRONG — argument order reversed
constructor(logger: Logger, sesConfig: SesConfig) { ... }

// WRONG — config read field by field instead of destructured
constructor(sesConfig: SesConfig, logger: Logger) {
  this._client = new SESv2Client(sesConfig.sesClientConfig);
  this._fromAddress = sesConfig.fromEmail ?? '';
}
```

A client that never logs takes no logger. That is a deliberate exception, not an oversight: such a client throws its errors to the caller instead of logging them.

The constructor may open a handle but must never perform I/O — see [Lifecycle](#lifecycle).

## Fields

Every field is `private` with a `_` prefix, declared in the same order the constructor assigns them. Nothing is public; expose things through getters.

```ts
// CORRECT
private _client: SESv2Client;
private _logger: Logger;

// WRONG — public field
public client: SESv2Client;

// WRONG — missing underscore
private client: SESv2Client;
```

## Config Shape

Fields passed **straight through** to the SDK keep the SDK's own type under a dedicated key. Values the client derives, converts, or defaults are flat fields.

```ts
// CORRECT — pass-through keeps the vendor type
export type S3Config = {
  s3ClientConfig: S3ClientConfig;
  bucket?: string;
  presignedUrlTtlSeconds?: number;
};

// CORRECT — flat, because the client transforms every value
export type PlatformConfig = {
  apiKey: string;
  scopes: string;   // split on ',' inside the client
  appUrl: string;   // parsed into host + scheme
  apiVersion: ApiVersion;
};

// WRONG — re-declaring options the SDK already types
export type S3Config = {
  region: string;
  accessKeyId?: string;
  secretAccessKey?: string;
  endpoint?: string;
  forcePathStyle?: boolean;
};
```

Re-declaring the vendor's options means every SDK upgrade is a second edit here, and every option you forgot to list is an option nobody can pass.

A client **never** receives the environment object, never sees an env variable name, and never reads `process.env`. Resolving one variable as a fallback for another, omitting credentials so the SDK falls back to an instance role, deriving `secure = port === 465` — all of that belongs to the consumer.

```ts
// WRONG — client knows env variable names
constructor(config: Environment, logger: Logger) {
  this._client = new SESv2Client({ region: config.SES_REGION || config.AWS_REGION });
}
```

## `static isConfigured`

A client that may legitimately be absent exposes `static isConfigured(config): boolean` — pure, taking the same config object — so the consumer can decide whether to construct it at all.

```ts
// CORRECT
static isConfigured(sesConfig: SesConfig): boolean {
  return Boolean(sesConfig.sesClientConfig.region && sesConfig.fromEmail);
}

// consumer
const mailer = SesClient.isConfigured(sesConfig) ? new SesClient(sesConfig, logger) : null;

// WRONG — instance getter answers the question too late to be useful
get isConfigured(): boolean {
  return this._client !== null;
}
```

## Pure Static Helpers

Transforms that touch no instance state are `private static`.

```ts
private static formatFromAddress(fromName?: string, fromEmail?: string): string {
  if (fromName && fromEmail) {
    return `"${fromName}" <${fromEmail}>`;
  }

  return fromEmail || '';
}
```

## Defaults

Defaults are `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` constants at the top of the module.

```ts
// CORRECT
const DEFAULT_PRESIGNED_URL_TTL_SECONDS = 300;
const DEFAULT_LOCK_TTL_MS = 10_000;

// WRONG — magic number inline
const uploadUrl = await getSignedUrl(this._client, command, { expiresIn: 300 });
```

## Exposing the Vendor Handle

When consumers need an escape hatch to the underlying object, expose it through a read-only getter — never as a public field.

```ts
get api(): Shopify {
  return this._api;
}
```

## Lifecycle

A client that owns a connection exposes `connect()` / `close()` / `quit()`. It never calls them itself — the consumer drives the lifecycle, typically from a shutdown hook.

```ts
// CORRECT
async connect(): Promise<void> { ... }
async close(): Promise<void> { ... }

// consumer
await database.connect();
onShutdown(async () => { await database.close(); });

// WRONG — I/O in the constructor: the caller cannot handle failure or ordering
constructor(databaseConfig: DatabaseConfig) {
  this._pool = new Pool(databaseConfig.masterPoolConfig);
  void this._pool.connect();
}
```

## Errors

Define the error class in the client file, extending `Error` with an explicit `this.name`. Never import the app's HTTP errors — mapping to a status code is the caller's job.

```ts
// CORRECT — s3.client.ts
export class S3NotConfiguredError extends Error {
  constructor(message = 'Image storage is not configured') {
    super(message);
    this.name = 'S3NotConfiguredError';
  }
}

// CORRECT — the caller maps it
try {
  return await this.storage.createPresignedUpload({ key, contentType });
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof S3NotConfiguredError) {
    throw new ServiceUnavailableError(error.message);
  }

  throw error;
}
```

## Logging

Log through `this._logger`, never `console`. Every message follows `[<Class_name>] <method_name>() <message>`, errors `[<Class_name>] <method_name>() error`, so one vendor's traffic stays greppable. See [logging-convention.md](../../core/logging-convention.md).

## Composition

A client receives other clients **through its config**; it never constructs one from environment values.

```ts
// CORRECT
export type PlatformConfig = {
  sessionStorage: SessionStorage;
  lockClient: RedlockClient;
};
```

Interchangeable clients share an interface declared next to the class that consumes them — `MailProviderClient` lives in `mail.client.ts`, and each provider client implements it.

## Collaborators

A helper class that serves exactly one client and cannot stand alone is a **collaborator**, not a client: file `{kebab-name}.ts` with no `.client.ts` suffix, class name with no `Client` suffix. It still takes `(config, logger)`.

```
clients/platform.client.ts              → PlatformClient   (wraps the SDK)
clients/platform-session-storage.ts     → SessionStorage
clients/platform-session-coordinator.ts → SessionCoordinator
```

The test: a client wraps an SDK connection of its own; a collaborator wraps none and exists to serve exactly one client. A collaborator may still be built at the composition root and handed to whatever needs it directly — that does not make it a client: it has no SDK of its own, no `static isConfigured`, and it never outlives the client it serves.

## Barrel

Every new client and collaborator is re-exported from the layer's `index.ts`. Let the import sorter order it rather than sorting by hand — its order is not plain ASCII.

## NEVER Do

- Name the class differently from the file (`s3.client.ts` exporting `StorageClient`).
- Name a client after its role in the app instead of the SDK it wraps.
- Export more than one primary client from a file.
- Rename our class to avoid a collision with the SDK — alias the vendor import instead.
- Fold the logger into the config object, or put it before the config.
- Accept the environment object, read `process.env`, or reference an env variable name inside a client.
- Import the app's HTTP error classes into a client.
- Touch request-scoped state — async local storage, a request object, a session from ambient context.
- Re-declare SDK options that the SDK already types — nest its config type instead.
- Answer "is this configured?" with an instance getter — use `static isConfigured`.
- Expose a public field, or hand out the vendor handle without a getter.
- Perform I/O in a constructor, or call `connect()` / `close()` from inside the client.
- Log with `console`, at the wrong level, or with a free-form message.
- Construct a dependency client from env inside another client — inject it via config.
- Forget to update the barrel.
